title: Celebrating My 30th And A Decade in Tech (2014–2024)
content:
I Just Turned Thirty and Spent the Last Decade Designing for Tech: Some Thoughts

Part coming to terms with this title, part gratitude as I look back, and a lot of hope some younger designer out there will read this and feel a bit more prepared for the future they’re inheriting.

2014–2024 was huge…I recognize that the world of work I started my career in in 2014 is different than today. And thats the point. I started work before AI was viable, before COVID decentralized workforces, before the 2021 capitol insurrection, before crypto and NFT attention economies, and before the Black Lives Matter movement. These events sent huge waves through how we work. As I lived through both the before and after these events, I offer the following to help provide important context to young creatives getting started.

I fully acknowledge that my work designing for tech companies is not representative of all industries. Additionally, here in the United States, we have been and will continue to face an agonizing uphill climb. Confrontation will be required. Change requires change. But, it also requires the technical skills to make it happen.

To you, the creative few who find my writing here applicable, I’ll start with this. Now is the time. Now is always the time. It always has been. Now is the time for slow reflection, planning, manifesting. Yes, of course. But damn, now is the time for our default behavior to be action. To get the idea out of your head, or your group text, and in to real life. Try the new thing, get in the habit of being brave, and say yes to having a coffee chat in person again. Get out the pencil and paper, be awful at first, build your skills, and build your focus. Trust me, you will get better.

1. Your life’s purpose is not just to consume

Humans are not just users — despite what every UX program or bootcamp told you in order to fill ‘hot jobs.’ I’m begging you, see through smoke and mirrors. Control your screen time and choose where your attention goes carefully. It’s so easy to sink into the rotted side of the internet. It’s hard to get out of it. If you can, avoid it all together. And if you’re already there, start following some accounts that feed your creative garden. Replace the trash with more references, interests, and creators who can be coaches on your way to your goals. As a starter for you, I’ll list some recent favorites that showed up on my feed at the bottom of this article. I keep the following idea close to heart, “You become the average of your six closest friends.” Not the best, not the worst, the average. I’ve found this to be so incredibly true. Surround yourself with influences who raise your average. For some that means going to college, for others that means meet ups like DC Design Week or communities like AIGA or ADP List. In a remote work environment, these outside voices are especially important. Pro tip, it may be time to delete your account and start fresh.

2. Nothing can replace practice

Hone your craft and avoid cheat codes while doing so. Learn how to collaborate with software and AI tools in a productive way by digging into the difference between your input and the output. Ask the right questions. Learn why blend modes are different in design tools. Ask for more explanation from your AI of choice. I promise you theres an interesting, and beautiful metaphor that our softwares are based off of. Find that foundational knowledge and understand it. It’ll help you apply your work better. For example, I’ve built digital products for most of my career, but I’ve always enjoyed interior design. Because I understand the principles of graphic design, which are inherently similar to principles for all design, I am able to apply those principles in new ways. In the last couple years I’ve been designing interior spaces for conferences, event booths, and office spaces. I am so thankful for the years and years of graphic design practice I had in order to be able to apply design to something totally new at work.

3. Nothing is new

I only want to speak about product design here, not the arts. We’ve polished enough crap that there are very few cases you should ever have to start from scratch. We’ll use designing websites as an example. I started designing websites in Photoshop, then Illustrator, then Sketch and Invision, then Figma or Webflow. Each of those softwares have done something a little better, a little more attuned to our end goal of designing a website. Here the software itself (Photoshop for web design) was the crap. We (UX designers and users) have provided feedback and evolved these tools as it’s passed between market leaders. Many many humans contributed to those interaction patterns over the last 50 years. Certain icons have become ubiquitous, expectations have generally been set and they should be designed for. And that’s human evolution, babes. Find a starting point, a reference, a component library and evolve it for something new, building off of what came before. I find myself spiritually connected to the work I pull from. And connected to that human who last pushed the turd uphill. I find it respectful; to say thank you for getting us here, I see you, and I’ll take it from here (then proceed to make the ugliest shit ever:)

4. Your taste will set you apart

Your taste will set you apart. Your craft will keep you employed. Both of these are necessary at the highest level you can muster. Especially as more and more people are able to generate work. Transparently, I don’t know how to teach taste. Come back to me at 35 and I’ll have a better answer. Craft though, meaning attention to detail, technical know-how, conceptual tightness, passion, are going to be the factors which set your work apart. It’s the way something feels when it’s “made with love” and where every detail has been considered and presented intentionally. Everyone’s got an opinion, a hot take (they probably heard somewhere else tbh), a POV. It’s all just noise until you are able to do something about it. I find myself now incredibly interested in the ‘how’ a piece came to life, not so much the product itself. We’re inundated with beautiful work everyday. I want to see the humanity and how you bent the machine to your will, not the other way around. Get used to the keyboard shortcuts, understand what’s happening under the hood, and master your craft.

5. Above all else, be kind

Advocate for others, amplify good ideas, and allow less wonderful ideas to fall to the wayside. Create opportunities for folks to succeed and check your ego at the door. Rather…check your ego at sign on.

Now in the early stages of the AI revolution, the careers of many humans are being eliminated. I encourage you to give your attention wisely; to put in the practice hours; to acknowledge those creatives work before you; to hone your taste and craft passionately; and to be good to each other. So much is changing for our species. These five points however, have served me, those before me, and I’d like to put my money on the resiliency of the human spirit as we continue.
